abstract: Pathology-image-to-gene-expression (P2G) studies often change the prediction head, image encoder, and spatial context together, making performance differences difficult to attribute. We examine these factors through paired image-input controls and explicit input regimes. Our main comparison covers five HEST-1K datasets, two 200-gene panels, and three selected held-out slides per dataset, using validation-selected checkpoints. Across all five datasets, replacing conventional image inputs with Virchow2 improves mean PCC-200 in 39 of 40 method--dataset--panel comparisons, while one comparison decreases. We introduce SimpleP2G, a direct gene-query decoder over frozen embeddings, and SimpleP2G-cross, which adds spatially positioned neighboring embeddings. With shared Virchow2 features, SimpleP2G has the highest single-patch mean PCC-200 on all five datasets under both panels; the cross-patch variant leads on four of five datasets under each panel. Decoder and context ablations show that greater depth and broader context do not consistently improve prediction. Together, these results suggest improving image representations before adding prediction-head complexity: a direct decoder over frozen pathology embeddings already provides a strong baseline. We hope our reimplemented image-encoder-upgraded baselines and SimpleP2G models serve as transparent, reproducible, and strong controls for future P2G research.
